comprehension.myAnswer: A Strand is an individual evidence package for a state transition. It contains: (1) a single Groth16 proof (three elliptic-curve group elements checked by a pairing equation), (2) the public claim (statement) that the proof attests to, where the proof's two public inputs carry a BLAKE2b digest of the statement bytes, and (3) context metadata tying the claim to a specific transaction step. From Sections 03 and 08, the statement bytes include compiled circuit constants (tag, family, predicate_digest, shape_digest, body_len) alongside transaction context fields in bytes 112..339 (vk_digest through intents_digest, including the spent state UTxO outref, its sequence number seq, the settlement script, the catalogue of permitted claims and verification keys, signed owner intents, and claimant_vkh). One Strand (one execution proof) can cover multiple required contract conditions. A Web is the complete collection of Strands required by a contract to authorize a single transaction; settlement enforces an all-or-nothing rule requiring every condition mandated by the contract for that action to be covered by a matching Strand in the Web.

comprehension.myAnswer: The Groth16 proof itself only proves that the prover knew a private witness satisfying the compiled R1CS constraints for two public inputs, which carry a BLAKE2b digest of the statement bytes. In the circuit, the transaction context fields (bytes 112..339, from vk_digest through intents_digest, including claimant_vkh) are supplied as free booleanized witness bits that are hashed by an in-circuit BLAKE2b gadget, not interpreted or verified against the ledger by the circuit. The actual connection to real Cardano transaction inputs and outputs is enforced on-chain at Layer 7 by the consuming settlement validator. First, during Issuance, the C2 claim policy checks the Groth16 pairing equation against the verification key and public inputs and mints a proof-claim UTxO holding a claim token (without checking whether the statement matches any live contract state or whether the claimant matches the statement). Second, at Settlement, the settlement transaction spends the contract thread UTxO and consumes all required proof-claim UTxOs (burning their claim tokens). The settlement validator rebuilds the expected statement bytes directly from the real transaction—using the spent thread UTxO outref, sequence number seq, custody snapshot and active duties in the thread datum, the catalogue_digest, the owner's signed intents (checking per-asset gross_cap, fee_cap, net_floor, liability_cap, validity window, and nonce = seq), the claimant_vkh, and the actual recipient and continuing-thread outputs—and checks that the rebuilt statement digest matches the verified digest in each consumed proof-claim UTxO. The validator also enforces actual output allocation (either strict one-output-per-obligation or a recomputed amount partition) and required signatures (claimants' signatures on settlement, plus owner intent authorizations). External facts like prices or delivery records are not authenticated by the proof and require an authenticated reference input or signer with explicit issuer and freshness rules.

(2) Step 1 — Owner signs limits: Before proving, the account owner signs an off-chain intent authorizing a 35 CASH partial payment. The intent fixes per-asset limits (gross_cap = 37 CASH, fee_cap = 2 CASH, net_floor = 35 CASH to the seller, and liability_cap), a validity window, a one-time nonce equal to the thread's sequence number (nonce = seq), and the target predicate_digest, vk_digest, and shape_digest. (3) Step 2 — Prover builds the Web: The prover executes the Moriarty invoice program action partial(35) over the private witness and generates the required Strand(s) covering three contract conditions: Condition 1 (Payment calculation: 100 CASH opening duty, 35 CASH seller payment, 37 CASH gross escrow debit), Condition 2 (Separate program fee: 35 CASH to seller, 2 CASH to program fee recipient, fee does not reduce invoice duty), and Condition 3 (Remaining obligations: 100 - 35 = 65 CASH unpaid invoice duty + 10 CASH unchanged reserve duty = 75 CASH total owed, with 75 CASH remaining in escrow custody). One whole-execution proof can cover all three conditions, tied to the spent state outref, seq, settlement script, catalogue, signed intents, and claimant_vkh. (4) Step 3 — Proof claims go on-chain (Issuance): For each Strand in the Web (n Strands = n Issue transactions), an Issue transaction is submitted. The C2 claim minting policy verifies one Groth16 proof and mints one proof-claim UTxO locking minimum ADA and a claim token with a claimant-chosen expiry. This does not spend the escrow UTxO or pay the seller. (5) Step 4 — Settlement: The Settlement transaction spends the escrow thread UTxO and consumes all required proof-claim UTxOs, burning their claim tokens and requiring each named claimant's signature. The settlement validator rebuilds the statement from the transaction, checks that all 3 required conditions are covered, checks the owner's signed intent caps/floors and validity window, and enforces the outputs: 35 CASH to the seller, 2 CASH to the fee recipient, and a continuing escrow thread UTxO holding 75 CASH with updated duties (65 CASH invoice, 10 CASH reserve) and incremented seq. (6) Inclusion, Finality, Readback & Recovery: The application/indexer confirms block inclusion, waits for required finality, and reads back the actual payment outputs and continuing thread duties to reconcile against the signed intent. If a submission times out, the outcome is treated as unknown rather than failed. comprehension.myAnswer: A condition (or required check / claim specification) is a logical rule defined by the contract that a state transition must satisfy—for instance, in the invoice payment, (1) payment calculation, (2) separate program fee, and (3) remaining obligations. A proof is the off-chain cryptographic Groth16 argument (three curve group elements) carried inside a Strand that attests the prover knew a witness satisfying a compiled circuit's constraints for a given statement digest. Crucially, conditions and proofs are not 1-to-1: a single whole-execution Groth16 proof (one Strand) can simultaneously satisfy multiple required contract conditions, or a Web can use multiple Strands (each carrying one proof) to cover different conditions. An on-chain claim output (proof-claim UTxO) is the ledger output minted on Cardano by an Issue transaction under the C2 claim policy after verifying one Groth16 proof. Each Strand requires its own Issue transaction on this route, so n Strands produce n on-chain claim outputs (each locking minimum ADA and holding a claim token). Creating an on-chain claim output only records verified evidence on-chain for a statement digest; it does not execute the financial transition, move escrow funds, or mint the application's token. Moreover, because C2 Issue does not check the statement against the live contract thread or verify that the claimant matches the statement, an on-chain claim output can exist on the ledger even if its claimant is mismatched, its target thread state has already been spent or revoked, or duplicate claim envelopes were minted for the same digest. Only when the Settlement transaction consumes all required claim outputs together, burns their claim tokens with the claimants' signatures, and matches their statement digests against the validator-rebuilt statement do those claim outputs authorize an actual state transition.

comprehension.myAnswer: What gets set up is the pair of public Groth16 keys—a proving key (used by the prover to generate proofs from a statement and witness) and a verifying key (used on-chain to check the pairing equation)—derived from secret randomness ('toxic waste') for a specific compiled circuit (its R1CS constraint matrices, bounds, and public-input layout). Because anyone retaining the secret randomness can forge proofs for false statements without a witness, soundness requires a trusted setup ceremony split into two phases where every phase's transcript verifies and at least one participant in each phase is honest and destroys their randomness. Phase 1 ('powers of tau') prepares universal parameters for a given elliptic curve, format, and circuit size capacity; it can be shared across all circuits that use the same curve and format and fit within that capacity. Phase 2 is circuit-specific and derives the proving and verifying keys for one distinct compiled circuit. To count setups: you count 1 shared Phase 1 per compatible curve/format parameter set (sized for the largest circuit) plus 1 Phase 2 stage per distinct compiled circuit, including any Groth16 wrapper circuits (for example, 5 distinct compatible circuits require 1 shared Phase 1 + 5 Phase 2 stages, which are stages rather than 5 + 1 full two-phase ceremonies). Changing transaction amounts, users, or public-input values does not require a new setup—the same keys are reused. However, changing the compiled rules, constraints, bounds, or public-input layout produces a new circuit that requires a new Phase 2 setup. Setups are counted by distinct compiled circuits (R1CS matrices), not by claim types, catalogue entries, application roles, or the 7 architectural layers, and there is no fixed Cardano-wide setup count without a frozen inventory of compiled circuits.

proseProblems.problem: In context, this passage (even with the brief note below it that 'Another partial payment would need another 2 CASH fee allowance') leaves the reader with the false impression that the invoice escrow state machine cleanly tracks and backs obligations through completion. In Section 08 ('Duties, backing and fees' and 'Invoice source, asset and funding comparison'), we learn that the contract has no top-up action to fund a second partial payment's 2 CASH fee and no reserve-duty-return action to discharge the 10 CASH reserve obligation after finish(), which permanently blocks the contract from closing. proseProblems.suggestedRewrite: The extra 2 CASH funds the fee for this single partial payment, leaving 75 CASH in escrow to match the 65 CASH unpaid invoice and the 10 CASH reserve obligation. Because each partial payment deducts another 2 CASH fee from escrow without reducing either obligation, an agreement that permits multiple partial payments must either pre-fund a fee allowance for the permitted number of partial steps or define a top-up action, and it must include a reserve-release action to reduce the 10 CASH reserve obligation to zero before the escrow account can close.

This output records checked evidence for later settlement. Step 3 does not mention that each Strand requires its own Issue transaction or that Issuance only checks the Groth16 proof for a statement digest (without checking live contract state or claimant binding), and Step 4 does not name the concrete transaction inputs/outputs from which the validator rebuilds the statement or how the indexer reconciles them against the signed intent.
proseProblems.suggestedRewrite: Step 3 / Proof claims go on-chain / For each Strand in the Web, an Issue transaction verifies one Groth16 proof against its verification key and mints one proof-claim UTxO holding minimum ADA and a claim token. This output records the verified statement digest, the named claimant and an expiry time, without spending the contract state or moving application funds. / Step 4 / The transaction settles / One settlement transaction spends the contract state UTxO and consumes every required proof-claim UTxO, burning each claim token with its claimant’s signature. The settlement validator rebuilds each expected statement digest from the spent state UTxO (outref, sequence number, custody balances and active duties), the owner’s signed intent limits and the actual recipient and continuing-state outputs, and verifies that it matches the digest in each consumed claim output. Once the block reaches required finality, the indexer reads back the recipient outputs and the continuing datum’s updated sequence number and obligations to reconcile them against the signed intent.

proseProblems.exactQuote: V2 SOURCE READING: tag, family, predicate_digest, shape_digest and body_len are circuit constants; the context fields vk_digest through intents_digest (bytes 112..339, including claimant_vkh) are free booleanized witness bits that are hashed, not interpreted. The consumer, not the circuit, ties those fields to the transaction: the settling validator rebuilds each statement from the transaction and the spent thread state, so a claim made for another thread step, catalogue, claimant or intent set does not match.
proseProblems.location: Section 08 ('What ties a Strand to its step')
proseProblems.problem: This is the crucial technical explanation of how a Groth16 proof is bound to a Cardano transaction, yet it is written in compressed audit shorthand ('free booleanized witness bits that are hashed, not interpreted') and leaves bytes 0..111 and the exact list of fields in bytes 112..339 unexplained. Rewriting it in clear technical prose makes the division of labor between the in-circuit BLAKE2b gadget and the on-chain validator immediately understandable.
proseProblems.suggestedRewrite: V2 SOURCE READING: A Strand’s statement is a fixed-layout byte string hashed inside the circuit by a BLAKE2b gadget into the proof’s two public inputs. The header fields (tag, family, predicate_digest, shape_digest and body_len) are compiled into the circuit as constants, while the transaction context fields in bytes 112..339—including vk_digest, catalogue_digest, the spent state’s outref and sequence number, claimant_vkh, and intents_digest—are passed into the circuit as unconstrained boolean witness bits solely so they are included in the BLAKE2b digest. The circuit itself does not check that those context bytes match the ledger; instead, at settlement the Cardano validator reconstructs the full statement byte string from the spent thread UTxO, the signed intents and the transaction outputs, hashes it, and requires it to equal the digest verified at issuance.

summary: Reading this page as an application operator maintaining an indexer, I can follow the high-level architecture of Webs and Strands, the two-step issuance-then-settlement route on Cardano, the arithmetic of the five example applications, why Groth16 requires a two-phase trusted setup counted per distinct compiled circuit, and the crucial division of labor where the circuit checks arithmetic over a statement digest while the on-chain settlement validator rebuilds the statement bytes from the transaction and enforces owner intent limits and claimant signatures. However, the page lacks the concrete operational and structural depth an indexer operator needs to actually track issuance, settlement, inclusion, finality, readback, and error recovery. Specifically: (1) it never shows the on-chain datum/redeemer schemas for contract threads or C2 proof-claim outputs, nor the complete byte layout of the statement (only mentioning in Section 08 that bytes 112..339 are free booleanized witness bits from vk_digest through intents_digest), leaving it unclear how an indexer correlates pending Issue UTxOs to a target contract thread before settlement; (2) it omits a transaction-by-transaction signer and funding matrix, explicitly admitting in Section 08 that the material does not state who signs an Issue transaction; (3) it tells operators to check inclusion, wait for finality, read back outputs/duties, and treat timeouts as unknown, but gives no deterministic rule for mapping raw transaction outputs (especially coalesced payments) back to specific signed intents or handling rollbacks; (4) its Section 08 notes reveal that the flagship S12 invoice program has no top-up action for a second partial payment's 2 CASH fee and no reserve-duty-return action to clear the 10 CASH reserve obligation after finish(), permanently blocking V2 Close; and (5) its visual diagrams do not teach the mechanics—Section 02 reuses the exact same 3-boxes-to-1-circle graphic across all five applications (visually conflating conditions with Strands and contradicting the single whole-execution proof model when toggling coverage), while Section 03 (settlement-stages.png) is just a 4-column text timeline with no UTxO flows, no n-to-1 Issue-to-Settle fan-in, and no Revoke/orphan/Reclaim recovery path.
